l: Extinction Characteristics of n-Alkane Droplets
x: Burning Modes of Three Fuels. n-heptane, n-decane, and n-dodecane: two-stage burning (hot and cool); n-dodecane at elevated pressure reaches three stages. n-decane: the ignition energy decides whether the hot flame forms, and radiative loss triggers the transition to a cool flame. With low ignition energy there is single-stage cool-flame burning, which depends on the flash point.

l: Extinction Characteristics of n-Alkane Droplets
x: Model and Validation. Droplet model with C7–C20 kinetics (583 species, 2609 reactions) and radiation. Measured and predicted extinction diameters are compared at 1 atm in air (slide 9). In the qualitative comparison for n-dodecane at 2.75 atm, the model parameters were not tuned (slide 6).

l: Extinction Characteristics of n-Alkane Droplets
x: Behavior at 1 atm in Air. At the transition to the second stage, the temperature and the stagnation ratio are nearly the same for the three fuels. A longer carbon chain gives a hotter cool flame (≈775 K for C12, 737 K for C10, 720 K for C7) and a smaller cool-flame extinction diameter. Hot-flame extinction barely changes between fuels (it is governed by small-species kinetics); cool-flame extinction does, and it is dictated by the decomposition of •O₂QOOH.

l: Extinction Characteristics of n-Alkane Droplets
x: Effect of Pressure. Up to 1 atm there are two stages; at 1.25 atm, repeated hot–cool–hot–cool cycles; at 3 atm, a stable "warm" flame. The cool-flame extinction diameter decreases with pressure and disappears at 3 atm, where the droplet burns completely.

l: Extinction Characteristics of n-Alkane Droplets
x: Conclusions. The transition to the second stage occurs universally near ~1200 K. Longer n-alkanes give more robust cool flames and smaller extinction diameters. The cool-flame extinction diameter varies linearly with the initial diameter, but it does not collapse onto a single curve as the hot-flame one does.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: Motivation. Relevant to engine knock and autoignition, the lean flammability limit, spacecraft fire safety, and low-temperature kinetics.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: Simulated Condition. 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet, 1 atm, 298 K, 10% O₂ and 5% O₃ with N₂ balance. 1D droplet model with detailed kinetics and narrow-band radiation.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: Observed Behavior. The ignition energy raises the local temperature above ~1150 K; the flame then expands and cools. It contracts in less than 0.1 s and the steady cool flame lasts only ~0.12 s (~710 K), after which it enters continuous oscillation.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: How the Oscillation Starts. Ozone locally raises the O₂ fraction (0.10 → 0.16), and this difference drives O₂ to diffuse outward, leaving a local void. The pulsations begin when the local O₂ falls below ~13.5%; the cycle repeats.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: Role of Low-Temperature Chemistry. The oscillation arises from the interplay between degenerate branching and QOOH propagation/termination, in the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) region.

l: Oscillatory Cool Flame in Sub-Millimeter Droplets
x: Fuel Leakage and Conclusion. Continuous fuel leakage through the flame makes the oscillation grow outward. With ozone the droplet attempts a steady cool flame but fails to achieve it and enters an ever-growing oscillation.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: What Is a Cool Flame. A ~650 K flame with weak reaction: it releases little heat, light, and CO₂. Davy observed it in 1817 (hot platinum wire in diethyl ether vapor); Emeléus recorded its emission and coined the term in 1929. Until 2012–2014 it was seen as a premixed-mixture phenomenon leading to ignition, typical of engine knock.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: The Discovery on the ISS (FLEX, 2011). In 2011, in the FLEX experiment on the International Space Station, a large n-heptane droplet showed "anomalous" combustion that was later identified as a cool flame on a droplet. This revived research on multiphase cool flames (2012–2014).

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Why the Cool Flame Appears. Radiative heat loss pushes the droplet from the first stage (hot flame) to the second (cool flame). A dynamic balance between heat generation and heat loss sustains the long-lasting cool-flame burning.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Kinetic Sensitivity and Revised Model. Increasing the rate of QOOHO₂ → QOOH + O₂ reduces the burning rate and increases the extinction diameter; the reaction QOOHO₂ → ketohydroperoxide + OH does the opposite. The next slide shows the evolution of the diameter and burning rate predicted with the revised kinetic model.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Multi-Stage Oscillatory Flames and Pressure. n-heptane model (4.08 mm, 3 atm, O₂/CO₂/N₂ = 0.21/0.15/0.64) with cycles of high-temperature ignition, radiative extinction, low-temperature reaction with self-heating, and reignition. The n-heptane ignition delay depends on pressure and on the degenerate branching in the kinetics (slide 17).

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
h: Three Stages with Helium Substitution (3 atm)
x: Three Stages with Helium Substitution (3 atm). More helium increases the burning rate; at high helium a quasi-steady third stage appears: hot (~950 K), moderate, and cool (~770 K). With more helium the second stage is suppressed; the droplet diameter barely changes because the flame contracts and compensates. Radiative and diffusive losses are comparable in the first two stages; in the third, diffusive losses dominate. Confirmed with n-dodecane at 2.75 atm (21.6% O₂, 50.2% N₂, 28.2% He): qualitative agreement with the model.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Small Droplets and Ozone. Question: can a cool flame be triggered in small droplets? Ozone helps, and a minimum concentration is needed to sustain combustion. Near-limit case (0.5 mm droplet, 1 atm, 298 K, 10% O₂, 5% O₃): the flame oscillates; the steady phase lasts only ~0.12 s at ~710 K.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Ground Experiments: Counterflow Diffusion Flame. It is an ideal configuration for studying flame strength under stretch and for validating kinetics and transport. The usual numerical approach (the one-dimensional OPPDIF module) assumes the results depend only on the axial coordinate and does not represent low-strain cool flames well. Buoyancy lifts the flame; a 2D model captures the flow perturbation and the effect of the Richardson number, and at higher strain the flame moves away from the nozzle.

l: Cool Flames in Space — PSI Seminar 2026
x: Summary and Current Status. The models were validated with FLEX data and then used to explore other scenarios. A large amount of experimental data remains to be interpreted.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
x: Dissertation Summary. Using CFD and detailed kinetics, it studies three topics: fire suppression in microgravity, refinement of butanol kinetic models, and cool flames initiated directly in small droplets.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
h: Ch. 2 — Droplet Combustion Model in Microgravity
x: Ch. 2 — Droplet Combustion Model in Microgravity. Formulation of the spherical model, gas- and liquid-phase equations, fiber, transport, and radiation.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
h: Ch. 3 — Xenon as a Fire Suppressant (background)
x: Ch. 3 — Xenon as a Fire Suppressant (background). With methanol as the model fuel, xenon lengthens the burning time and raises the flame temperature; it sustains a hot flame with less oxygen. Its low thermal diffusivity makes it a worse suppressant; NASA postponed testing it.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
h: Chs. 4 and 5 — Butanol and Its Isomers (background)
x: Chs. 4 and 5 — Butanol and Its Isomers (background). The model of Sarathy et al. predicted burning that was too fast; a perturbation analysis pointed to the transport parameters of each isomer. After updating them, the predictions improved significantly.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
x: Ch. 6 — Ozone-Assisted Cool Flame. Ozone releases atomic oxygen, produces extra heat, and stabilizes the cool flame near the droplet. The flash point decides: n-decane tends toward damped oscillation and requires more ozone than n-heptane.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
h: Ch. 7 — Oscillatory Cool Flame Near the Limit
x: Ch. 7 — Oscillatory Cool Flame Near the Limit. Near the limit the flame does not reach steady burning and oscillates ever more strongly; this is caused by QOOH chemistry and fuel leakage.

l: Doctoral Dissertation of M. F. Alam (USC, 2018)
x: Ch. 8 — Conclusion. Droplet simulations are useful for predicting extinction with untested suppressants, validating and refining kinetics, and understanding cool flames in sub-millimeter droplets.

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
h: Cool Flames Triggered by Radiative Losses
x: Cool Flames Triggered by Radiative Losses. First observed in n-heptane droplets on the ISS (2011); with CO₂ as diluent, radiative losses increase and multi-stage burning appears.

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
x: The Question: More Diffusive Losses. Slide 5 poses the question of whether conditions that increase diffusive losses and reactivity (helium as diluent and higher pressure) affect burning. A transient droplet model is used, with detailed high- and low-temperature kinetics and radiation.

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
h: Three Stages with Helium at 3 and 5 atm
x: Three Stages with Helium at 3 and 5 atm. More helium raises the burning rate and a quasi-steady third stage appears. At high helium the second stage is suppressed. At 5 atm the same behavior is seen, but with more helium. The flame contraction keeps the droplet diameter nearly the same despite the temperature drop. Heat generation and losses are strongly coupled; diffusive losses dominate the third stage.

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
x: Kinetics and Species. Low-temperature (QOOH) chemistry is what predominates in the third stage. There is competition between adding O₂ to QOOH and decomposing QOOH (OH, HO₂, olefins, carbonyls).

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
x: Experimental Confirmation in FLEX. FLEX 1268: n-dodecane, 2.75 atm, 21.6% O₂, 50.2% N₂, 28.2% He, with qualitative agreement with the predictions. FLEX 1256: n-dodecane, 3.00 atm, air, ~4.2 mm droplet.

l: Three-Stage Burning: Hot, Warm, and Cool
x: Conclusions. There are two quasi-steady cool-flame modes in droplets: "warm" (NTC regime) and "cool" (low temperature). Helium is critical: it either promotes or completely suppresses the second stage. The n-dodecane experiments validate the a priori prediction made with n-heptane.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 1. What a cool flame is. According to the general presentation (slide 3, citing Wikipedia), a cool flame has a typical temperature of ~650 K and its reaction is not vigorous: it releases little heat, light or carbon dioxide. The same slide recounts that in 1817 Humphry Davy introduced a hot platinum wire into a mixture of air and diethyl ether vapor and obtained pale phosphorescent light in the dark; in 1929 Harry Julius Emeléus recorded its emission spectra and coined the term "cool flame". Before 2012–2014 the traditional view (slide 4) associated cool flames with premixed combustion leading to ignition of hot fuel-air mixtures, such as engine knock. The oscillatory presentation (slide 2) lists as practical relevance: engine knock and multistage autoignition, the lean flammability limit, spacecraft fire safety, and low-temperature/NTC kinetics.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 2. FLEX and "anomalous" combustion. The three-stage presentation (slide 2) identifies the FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) experiments on the International Space Station in 2011 (ref. Nayagam et al., 2012) as the first observation of "cool flames" in n-heptane droplet diffusion flames. The general presentation (slide 32) calls it "anomalous combustion" of a large n-heptane droplet. The article by Farouk and Dryer (2014), cited in the presentations, describes the combustion of an isolated n-heptane droplet in microgravity as two-stage combustion with "cool flames". Slides 32–34 speak of a "resurgence" of cool flame research (2012 and 2014).

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 3. What sustains the cool flame. General presentation (slide 7): radiative heat loss pushes the system toward the transition to the second stage, the cool flame stage; a dynamic balance between heat generation and heat loss sustains the cool flame for a long time. Extinction presentation (slide 16): the transition to the second stage occurred, for all three fuels, at a peak flame temperature of ~1200 K. Kinetic sensitivity (general presentation, slide 8): increasing the rate of QOOHO₂ → QOOH + O₂ decreased the burning rate and increased the extinction diameter; with QOOHO₂ → ketohydroperoxide + OH the opposite occurs. The next slide presents predictions with a revised kinetics.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
h: 4. Three stages with helium and pressure
x: 4. Three stages with helium and pressure. General presentation (slides 13–18), 4.00 mm n-heptane, 21% O₂, 3 atm: replacing part of the N₂ with helium increases the burning rate and, with more helium, a quasi-steady third stage appears. Stages: high temperature; moderate temperature (~950 K); low temperature (~770 K). With more helium the second stage is suppressed. The droplet diameter hardly changes between stages because the flame contracts. Radiative and diffusive losses are comparable in stages 1 and 2; in the third, diffusive losses dominate. At 5 atm with more helium similar behavior is observed (three-stage presentation, slide 20). Experiments: the general presentation shows n-dodecane at 2.75 atm (21.6% O₂, 50.2% N₂, 28.2% He) with qualitative agreement between prediction and observation. The three-stage presentation (slides 21–22) is titled "Experimental Observation of 3 Stage Behavior" and cites FLEX 1256: n-dodecane, 3.00 atm, 21% O₂, 79% N₂, Do ≈ 4.2 mm (I did not read the graphical content of those slides). Summary of that presentation (slide 17): there are two quasi-steady cool flame modes, "warm" (NTC regime) and "cool" (low temperature); the helium concentration is critical because it promotes or suppresses the second stage. Note: that presentation acknowledges grants NNX14AG461A and NNX09AW19A, not NNX17AF97A.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 5. Extinction: fuel and pressure. Extinction presentation (slide 16, summary): all three fuels show a hot-to-cool transition; hot flame extinction is very similar among them; cool flame extinction depends on molecular weight: longer n-alkanes have a more robust (hotter) cool flame and smaller extinction diameters. The cool flame extinction diameter varies linearly with the initial droplet diameter, but does not collapse onto a single function as the hot flame one does. Pressure (slides 12, 13 and 15): ≤1 atm, two stages; at 1.25 atm, repeated hot-cool cycles (four transitions in 7 mm n-dodecane; with each one the cool flame temperature drops and the burning time rises); at 3 atm, a stable "warm" flame dominated by NTC kinetics and competition for OH. The cool flame extinction diameter decreases with pressure and does not exist at 3 atm because the droplet burns out completely. The extinction presentation also reports peak cool flame temperatures of ~720 K (n-heptane), ~737 K (n-decane) and ~775 K (n-dodecane).

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 6. Small droplets and ozone. Thesis, 6.5: n-heptane and n-decane (low and high flash point) were studied by simulation, with 0.1 and 0.5 mm droplets, at 1 and 25 atm and with ambient ozone (O₃). Goal: to see whether a direct cool flame can be established where radiative extinction is unlikely. Results noted in that section: the required ignition energy differs between low and high flash point fuels; without ozone, in the low flash point fuel it is hard to avoid the transition to a hot flame; in the high flash point fuel, controlling the ignition energy can yield a cool flame without a hot flame; with O₃ the reaction onset temperature is reduced; there is a minimum O₃ concentration for a quasi-steady cool flame and a maximum above which a hot flame always occurs. Important: these are numerical results.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 7. Oscillatory flames. Oscillatory presentation (slide 13, summary) and thesis 7.5: 0.5 mm n-heptane droplet, 1 atm, with reduced O₂ (10%) and 5% O₃. The droplet briefly attempts a stable cool flame and then enters continuous oscillatory cool flame. The onset of oscillation is triggered by local O₂ depletion (below 13.5% according to the presentation; below 12% according to the thesis). The oscillation grows with each cycle. It is attributed to the interaction between degenerate branching and QOOH propagation/termination (NTC regime) and to the continuous leakage of fuel through the flame. Thesis 7.5: at 21% O₂ with 5% O₃ the droplet reaches a direct cool flame. The oscillation is pronounced with little ozone and decreases as ozone increases. These are numerical results.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 8. 1 g simulation: counterflow and buoyancy. General presentation (slides 25–31), based on Saha and Farouk (2026): the usual 1D module (OPPDIF/CHEMKIN) assumes a linear radial velocity and variables that depend only on the axial coordinate. The slide notes that cool flames correspond to low Reynolds number, low strain rate (~100 s⁻¹) and finite flame thickness. With buoyancy, the flame rises. Without it, 1D and 2D place the flame near the stagnation plane. For the DME case shown, the peak temperature is somewhat lower in 1D and the temperature gradient is larger (more diffusive loss). At higher global strain rate, the flame moves away from the nozzle until buoyancy is negligible. Summary (slide 31): the models were validated against FLEX data and then used to explore other scenarios.

l: PSI-117 — Cool flames in microgravity (interpreted)
x: 9. Limits and what remains unresolved. Without ozone, in low flash point fuels it is hard to avoid the hot flame (thesis 6.5). Above a certain ozone concentration a hot flame always occurs (thesis 6.5). Near the limit, the cool flame does not stabilize: after a brief quasi-steady period it enters continuous oscillation (oscillatory presentation, thesis 7.5). The three-stage predictions were compared with observations only qualitatively. The thesis (8.2) says it explains the direct establishment of a cool flame with ozone in order to encourage drop-tower tests; the ozone and oscillation results of sections 6 and 7 are numerical. I did not find, in the presentations or in chapters 6 and 7, specific results of the forced 3-D model (convection, heating) that the PSI-117 metadata describe. That is not included here.

l: PSI-62: concurrent flame spread modeling
x: PSI-62. Combustion Science and spacecraft fire safety investigation. Concurrent flame spread in microgravity; BASS and BASS-II; flamelet generated manifold FGM and unsteady FGM UFGM; coupled fluid-solid response, charring, and ablation; flat sheets, spheres, PMMA rods, and wax cylinders. Two-color tomography with DSLR cameras reconstructs three-dimensional temperature and soot fields. Comparison metrics include flame geometry, temperature, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate. Goldilocks flammability zone. Objective: predict spacecraft material flammability limits and develop subgrid-scale models for fire simulations. PSI-62 metadata.
